items._ogDesc: United Airlines said Monday that it was experiencing a systemwide outage that was affecting departing flights, just days after a malfunction in the Federal Aviation Administration’s network prompted a nationwide ground stop.
items.body:
CHICAGO — United Airlines said Monday that it had resolved a technology issue that delayed departing flights, just days after a malfunction in the Federal Aviation Administration’s network prompted a nationwide ground stop.

Chicago-based United said in a statement that while some flights were delayed because of the issue Monday afternoon, flights that were in the air and flights on its United Express regional network were not impacted. It also said, “There is no indication that this was a cybersecurity-related issue.”

United apologized to customers for the inconvenience on social media. It resolved the issue about 1 1/2 hours after pilots first began reporting problems to air traffic controllers.

United did not immediately provide details about which of the airlines systems were affected, but pilots told air traffic controllers that the problem was related to United’s system that helps them determine a plane’s final weight to ensure it can safely take off.

A recording posted on the ATC app showed a United pilot in Houston asking the tower for permission to stay put at the gate until the system was working again. The app combines live air traffic control radio feeds with real-time visual aircraft tracking.

The flight tracking website FlightAware showed United with 418 delayed flights late Monday afternoon.

The United computer problem is just the latest high-profile technology meltdown in recent days.

Earlier Monday, thousands of people reported being unable to access their online accounts at several major U.S. banks after JPMorgan Chase had a technical problem.

On Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration ordered every flight grounded because a new router that was installed malfunctioned and overwhelmed the aging air traffic control system. And one day earlier, Microsoft experienced a major disruption to its Outlook email service. Microsoft said Saturday that services were fully restored.

Josh Funk, The Associated Press

items.title: Food safety concerns spark warning, recalls in Canada
items.description: Some food and beverage products are being recalled in Canada due to food safety concerns for issues such as the presence of insects and metal pieces.

items._ogDesc: Some food and beverage products are being recalled in Canada due to food safety concerns for issues such as the presence of insects and metal pieces.
items.body:
Some food and beverage products are being recalled in Canada due to food safety concerns for issues such as the presence of insects and metal pieces.

The Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA) recently posted recalls and a food safety warning on its website for the following products.

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

Producers brand brown rice

Tree of Life Canada is recalling its Producers brand brown rice because of the “presence of insects,” according to the CFIA’s advisory.

“Do not use, sell, serve or distribute the affected product,” the CFIA warned.

The affected products are 22.6 kg packages of brown rice with the Universal Product Codes (UPC) 0 72806 00225 0, and the following codes:

  • 11/09/26, 13326PRM
  • 11/10/26, 13426PRM
  • 12/12/26, 16626PRM
  • 12/14/26, 16826PRM

The product was sold to hotels, restaurants and institutions in Alberta, British Columbia, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, Nova Scotia, Ontario and Quebec.

The CFIA designated it a Class 3 recall. This type of recall means there’s “a low risk that consuming the food may result in any undesirable health problems,” or it “includes food that do not pose a health risk, but that do not comply with legislation.”

Cold Grind organic turmeric powder

The federal agency issued a food safety warning for the Cold Grind brand of organic turmeric powder. It said the product may be unsafe due to the non-permitted colour Sudan I.

“Do not consume, use, sell, serve or distribute affected products,” the CFIA said in a notice online.

The warning is for all 50 g packages with the UPC 6 28110 34220 1.

Those who believe they got sick from consuming the product are advised to contact their health-care provider.

The CFIA said its test results sparked the warning, adding that no illnesses were reported.

“The Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA) is conducting a food safety investigation, which may lead to the recall of this or other products,” the advisory said.

Archibald’s Nuit Blanche White IPA beer

The Archibald brand Nuit Blanche White IPA is being recalled due to the presence of metal pieces.

“Do not use, sell, serve or distribute the affected products,” according to the CFIA notice.

The following are the affected beer products sold in Quebec:

  • 473 ml pack with UPC 8 76976 00075 3 and all codes starting with J28Q61
  • 4 x 473 ml with UPC 8 76976 00078 4, with codes starting with J28Q61

Quebec-based Archibald Inc. issued the Class 3 recall.

Among other products recently recalled include the popular beers Molson Canadian, Coors Light, Blue Moon due to the presence of metal pieces. The recall covers several alcoholic and non-alcoholic beers made by parent company Molson Canada 2005.

With files from CTV News’ Daniel Otis

items.title: Staff exodus hits Poilievre’s office as new B.C. Conservative government goes on hiring spree
items.description: Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre’s top communications staff are leaving his office to join the new Conservative government in B.C. with four sources saying all in about half a dozen aides could leave the federal Conservatives.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre delivers a speech on national unity in Calgary, Friday, Oct. 16, 2026. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Jeff McIntosh]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Jeff McIntosh</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre’s top communications staff are leaving his office to join the new Conservative government in B.C. with four sources saying all in about half a dozen aides could leave the federal Conservatives.
items.body:
OTTAWA — Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre’s top communications staff are leaving his office to join the new Conservative government in B.C., with sources saying about half a dozen aides could leave the federal Conservatives.

Four sources with knowledge of the internal changes said Poilievre’s director of communications, Micah Green, and his director of media relations, Sam Lilly, have both decided to leave.

They are taking jobs in B.C. Premier-designate Lorne Doerkson’s new government, the sources said.

The sources also said Doerkson’s team is in the middle of an intense hiring blitz as it tries to staff-up after winning last month’s snap election.

They said because the new B.C. government is still hiring, the precise number of people leaving the Opposition Leader’s Office is not yet confirmed, though three of the sources said they expected it to be around half a dozen staff. They also said Doerkson’s team is hiring staff from Alberta Premier Danielle Smith’s government.

CTV News is not identifying the sources who were not authorized to disclose information on the hiring decisions.

One of the sources noted that both Lilly and Green, who are from B.C., are returning home. But, their exits come on the heels of several other high-profile resignations.

On Nov. 5, CTV News reported that Poilievre’s deputy chief of staff Aaron Wudrick was also leaving the Conservative leader’s team. Wudrick’s exit will be official at the end of the month.

Green is Poilievre’s second director of communications to quit this year. In April, Katy Merrifield quit the same post and ended up running Doerkson’s come-from-behind majority government victory.

‘Returning home’: Green

In a statement to CTV News on Monday, Green wrote that he has accepted a job with the B.C. government and is “returning home” to the province as he and his wife expect their first child.

“Working for Pierre Poilievre has been the honour of my career,” Green wrote. “The first door I ever knocked on was for Pierre, and I met my wife knocking doors for him.”

“I owe him an enormous amount, both personally and professionally,” he added, also writing the Conservative leader has his “full support.”

Also in a statement to CTV News on Monday, Lilly wrote that he’ll be starting an “exciting new journey” with the B.C. government next month, noting his “roots are in British Columbia.”

“Having the pleasure of serving three leaders in the (Oppositon Leader’s Office) is a rare and exceptional privilege,” Lilly wrote. “I have made so many friends and earned a lifetime of experience.”

“Parting ways is never easy, but I leave with tremendous gratitude and thanks in my heart,” he also wrote, adding Poilievre has his support.

Email confirms two other departures

In an internal email obtained by CTV News, Poilievre’s chief of staff, Steve Outhouse, wished Green and Lilly “all the best,” and confirmed two more departures: Poilievre’s scheduler and executive assistant Hayley Quipp, and senior policy adviser Andrew Evans.

Outhouse wrote that Quipp, as Green’s wife, is also headed to B.C., while Evans is taking a job in the private sector.

The chief of staff thanked Green and Lilly for their “tireless efforts,” celebrated Quipp’s commitment, and added that Evans has “shown a commitment to quality of work that is appreciated.”

“More information about new team members will follow in due course,” Outhouse wrote.

Departures present fresh challenges for Poilievre

The timing will present fresh challenges for the embattled Conservative leader, whose party is facing a tough byelection race on Dec. 7.

Poilievre is trying to hang on to his party’s seat in Brantford-Brant South, but amid high public support for Prime Minister Mark Carney, polling suggests a toss-up between the Liberals and Conservatives.

In recent weeks, Conservative sources have told CTV News that the pressure will start to mount on Poilievre’s leadership if the Conservatives lose the race in southwestern Ontario.

Despite having been on the cusp of forming government ahead of the 2025 federal election, Poilievre’s party and his own personal popularity numbers have since languished in the polls.

Since Carney’s election last year, a wave of eight Conservative MPs have left the party. Four of them crossed the floor to the Liberals, which allowed Carney to secure a majority government.

Over the summer, meanwhile, 17 Conservative MPs from across the country spoke to CTV News about their concerns about Poilievre and the party’s prospects.

Still, Poilievre said earlier this month he will stay on as leader even if the party loses the Brantford–Brant South byelection.

Also on Monday, Poilievre’s inner circle of MPs extended an invitation — which has been obtained by CTV News — to the Conservative caucus to a cocktail hour in their Parliament Hill office on Tuesday evening for “discussion, refreshments, and snacks.”

With files from CTV News’ Stephanie Ha

items._ogDesc: Twenty-five former cabinet ministers and former heads of parliament in Ecuador are warning the some provisions of the Canada-Ecuador free trade deal are putting the countries’ economic relationship at risk.
items.body:
OTTAWA — Twenty-five former cabinet ministers and former heads of parliament in Ecuador are warning that some provisions of the Canada-Ecuador free trade deal are putting the countries’ economic relationship at risk.

The two countries signed a free trade deal in July, with several Canadian organizations and civil society leaders warning it will threaten the environment and worsen a human rights crisis in the South American country.

In a letter to International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu, 25 Ecuadorian politicians object to the inclusion of investor-state dispute settlement provisions in the deal and urge the government to remove those sections before ratifying it.

The letter said the provisions, which would allow foreign investors to sue governments through an international tribunal instead of through domestic sovereign courts, are unconstitutional in Ecuador and have been rejected by Ecuadorian voters in several referendums.

“We are not opposed to Canadian investment in Ecuador or to closer economic relations between our two countries,” said the letter. “We write because we believe this agreement, as currently structured, places that relationship at risk.”

The Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives says the provisions were requested by the mining industry and opposed by human rights organizations during public consultations held in 2023.

Stuart Trew, the organization’s senior researcher, said investor-state dispute settlement provisions won’t enhance investment in either country.

“It just gives these companies a real sharp tool they can use to basically threaten countries away from policies they don’t want to see introduced,” said Trew. “We’re quite alarmed by what the Canadian government has done here.”

The Canadian Press has reached out to the federal government for comment but has not .yet received a response.

The letter said Canada and Ecuador have substantial shared interests in trade, investment and development, but the politicians urge caution about “an instrument likely to be contested for the duration of its life.”

“An agreement built on sound legal and democratic foundations will serve the relationship between our countries considerably better than one that invites constitutional challenge from the day it enters into force,” said the letter.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 16, 2026.

Catherine Morrison, The Canadian Press

items.title: Telus sees ‘serious concerns’ with Quebecor’s $31B takeover bid
items.description: Quebecor Inc. is proposing a merger with Telus Corp. in a deal valued at about $31 billion, but competition concerns could stand in the way of a potential transaction.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Quebecor Inc. is proposing a strategic combination with Telus Corp. in a cash-and-stock deal valued at about $31 billion. (Left: Getty Images, Right: Canadian Press)]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: Quebecor Inc. is proposing a merger with Telus Corp. in a deal valued at about $31 billion, but competition concerns could stand in the way of a potential transaction.
items.body:
MONTREAL — The chief executive of Quebecor Inc. says his company’s proposed $31-billion takeover of Telus Corp. is meant to drive efficiencies and free up cash to spend on new infrastructure, while dismissing concerns that a merger would lead to deteriorating competition in the telecommunications sector.

Quebecor revealed Monday it is proposing the merger with Telus in a cash-and-stock deal. The Montreal-based company said a potential deal would combine complementary networks, spectrum and operations to boost investment capacity and create a more competitive company.

“Our transaction is not based on increasing revenues, it’s certainly not based on increasing prices,” said Quebecor president and CEO Pierre Karl Péladeau in an interview.

“Our transaction is to generate savings, to generate synergies that will be able for us ... to reduce the amount of debt, but also to make sure that we will have the financial resources to invest in other networks.” 

  • Latest updates on company news here

Péladeau said the Canadian telecom sector is vulnerable to the threat of foreign players taking market share. He pointed to American companies like SpaceX, whose satellite internet service known as Starlink has been gaining ground in Canada as it poaches customers from established providers.

“If we were not to have Canadian operators that are financially strong, ... we should think about what’s going to happen down the road. In the meantime, it’s time to do something,” Péladeau said.

“When you’re joining those companies together ... you’re going to be able maybe to take those financial resources and invest in another type of network which is also going to be the network of the future.”

Quebecor estimates the proposed takeover would create around $160 million in annual operating cost savings and $235 million in annual capital savings, on top of Telus’ recently announced goal of achieving approximately $900 million in savings per year moving forward from the end of 2028.

It said those efficiencies would support new spending on network upgrades, integration with Canadian satellite networks and service enhancements. It would also go toward the deployment of artificial intelligence, data centres and advanced connectivity infrastructure.

But Telus chief executive Victor Dodig said in an interview that the company has “serious concerns” with Quebecor’s proposal, with the “largest hurdle” being regulatory issues. 

He said the offer also “doesn’t nearly reflect the value of Telus.”

“I think this is all about the resilience, strength, sovereignty and safety of the telecom sector in Canada. This does not advance that at all,” said Dodig, who took the helm at Telus in July.

  • Latest updates on investing here

Telus said its board of directors has formed a special committee of independent directors to review and evaluate the Quebecor proposal and explore other strategic alternatives.

Asked about Quebecor’s goal of finding savings so that a potential combined company could spend more on infrastructure and new technologies, Dodig said that’s something his company already has “completely under control.”

“In my estimation, every single point of their offer has serious complications,” he said.

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said in a statement on Monday that the transaction will be “rigorously reviewed.”

“We will not predetermine the outcomes of the reviews related to this or any other specific transaction,” the statement said. 

“In the face of accelerating technological change, global instability and ongoing cost-of-living pressures, the Government of Canada will relentlessly prioritize the best interests of Canadians and Canadian sovereignty.”

Quebecor said it made a non-binding proposal to Telus on June 26 to serve as the basis for negotiations and then submitted what it called an “enhanced proposal” on Nov. 9.

Under the offer, Telus shareholders would receive $6.35 in cash and 0.17 class B shares of Quebecor for each Telus share. Quebecor said the bid is worth $19.45 per share based on its closing share price on Friday. Telus shares closed at $12.14 on Friday.

Despite Dodig arguing the offer undervalues Telus, Péladeau said he believes the offer is fair based on the company’s share price.

“The market is valuing their shares at $12. It’s not me, it’s the market,” he said.

“I mean (Dodig’s) been there for what, three, four months now, even more? In fact, the stock went further down than up.”

Scotiabank analyst Maher Yaghi said a potential deal would face significant obstacles, pointing to likely reviews by the Competition Bureau, the CRTC and Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada. He said additional federal reviews or approvals could also be required “given the strategic nature of Canadian telecommunications infrastructure.”

Telus noted that even if such a deal received regulatory approvals, it may be subject to certain conditions that “materially affect the combined company.” 

If a merger between Quebecor and Telus moved forward, it would be the largest takeover in Canada’s telecom sector since Rogers Communications Inc. purchased Shaw in 2023.

As part of that $26-billion transaction, Quebecor’s Videotron subsidiary acquired Freedom Mobile from Shaw. Rogers and Shaw agreed to sell Freedom to Videotron to ease competition concerns raised by the original proposal.

Both of those transactions came with a list of conditions meant to protect competition in the telecom sector. They included Rogers establishing a second headquarters in Calgary and adding 3,000 new jobs based in Western Canada that it must maintain for at least 10 years.

Rogers was also required to spend billions to expand 5G coverage and additional network services, as well as to connect rural, remote and Indigenous communities.

Dodig said Telus is drawing lessons from the Rogers-Shaw merger, which took more than two years to come to fruition after it was initially proposed as the companies involved worked to address government and regulatory concerns.

“We’re all modernizing our businesses, our way of life. The telecom sector and Telus’ role in it needs to kind of stay at the forefront, not get caught up in some sort of regulatory morass that’s going to take years,” Dodig said.

As part of the Rogers-Shaw merger, Videotron was required to offer plans at least 20 per cent lower than its competitors and spend $150 million over two years to upgrade Freedom Mobile’s network. It is also restricted from transferring any Freedom Mobile licences for a decade.

Quebecor said that it “has fully performed the undertakings it made” to Ottawa since that deal, while demonstrating its ability “to combine growth, pro-consumer pricing and innovation.” It noted that wireless prices fell 35.4 per cent in the three years following the acquisition of Freedom, according to Statistics Canada.

“Of all the obligations we took, we even delivered them faster. There’s no reason we will change. Our track record is there to show what we are able to do,” Péladeau said.

“If we were to take other obligations, we’ll listen to ISED, we’ll listen to the (Competition) Bureau and we will do what is appropriate to make sure that we will be then generating resources that will make this company and this country stronger.”

  • How to set BNN Bloomberg as your preferred source on Google

Péladeau said Quebecor has discussed the potential merger with federal regulators and planned to meet with Dodig next Monday to discuss further steps.

But combining two of Canada’s four largest wireless service providers “would undo the competitive structure regulators set up when they required Freedom to be divested as part of the Rogers-Shaw approval,” Scotiabank’s Yaghi said in a note.

“Without meaningful remedies, the deal runs against the government policy intent behind the Freedom transaction,” he said, adding that approval could be contingent on Quebecor offering “significant concessions to the government” to keep telecom prices low.

“Regulatory decisions will make or break the deal, not price. If Quebecor is not ready to let go of Freedom Mobile, we believe this deal has a low chance of going through.”

Quebecor’s share price fell about 15 per cent or $11.81 to $65.25 in trading on Monday. Telus’ share price was up about 13 per cent or $1.56 to $13.70.

Sammy Hudes, The Canadian Press

items.title: Carney says Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if Trump trade talks fail
items.description: Prime Minister Mark Carney said Monday that Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with U.S. President Donald Trump fail to preserve an integrated North American auto industry.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Prime Minister Mark Carney walks past an honour guard as he arrives in Shenzen, China, Monday, Nov. 16, 2026. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Adrian Wyld]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Adrian Wyld</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Prime Minister Mark Carney said Monday that Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with U.S. President Donald Trump fail to preserve an integrated North American auto industry.
items.body:
PHNOM PENH, Cambodia -- Prime Minister Mark Carney said Monday that Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with U.S. President Donald Trump fail to preserve an integrated North American auto industry.

Carney’s comments in Cambodia came ahead of a planned meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping this week in Shenzhen, China, where Chinese auto manufacturing is expected to be discussed. The two leaders reached an agreement in January allowing tens of thousands of Chinese electric vehicles into Canada at reduced tariffs.

“We have the best auto workers in the world, and we want them fully deployed, full opportunity, in an integrated North American market,” Carney told reporters in Cambodia. “That market has become less integrated because of U.S. trade actions.”

Carney said Saturday in Manila, Philippines, that any trade agreement with Washington must leave Canada with a viable auto industry. He said Monday that negotiations with the United States remain his priority, but their outcome could determine whether Canada pursues alternatives involving European, Chinese or Japanese automakers.

Asked whether potential Chinese investment was leverage in the U.S. negotiations, Carney replied: “It’s not leverage. But action, reaction” on behalf of Canada’s auto workers and manufacturing assets.

“If they’re not fully utilized in a North American context, that provides other opportunities,” Carney said. “Canada is going to move forward either way.”

White House trade adviser Peter Navarro lashed out on social media Monday in response to Carney’s suggestion that Canada could turn to Chinese automakers.

“Are u really threatening to play China off the U.S.? This is offensive in the extreme,” Navarro wrote on X. “You should be far more worried China is going to eat Canada alive.”

The Detroit Three -- Ford, General Motors and Stellantis -- operate factories across Canada, the United States and Mexico, with parts sometimes crossing borders multiple times before a vehicle is completed. Trump has repeatedly pushed automakers to move production to the United States from Canada.

Carney said any Chinese investment would have to involve substantial manufacturing in Canada rather than simply assembling imported parts. He said it would require proper labor standards, manufacturing facilities and domestic supply chains that expand over time, including the use of Canadian critical minerals in electric vehicles.

“It’s not just about kit cars,” he said. “There has to be a manufacturing aspect involved.”

Under the January agreement, Canada reduced its 100 per cent tariff on Chinese electric vehicles to 6.1 per cent, initially allowing up to 49,000 vehicles annually, with the cap increasing over time. In exchange, China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola.

Carney said at the time that he expected the agreement to attract Chinese investment in Canada’s auto industry and create jobs.

The deal drew criticism from Ontario Premier Doug Ford, whose province is the centre of Canada’s auto industry. Ford warned that allowing Chinese electric vehicles into Canada could threaten Canadian jobs and jeopardize access to the U.S. market.

“The federal government’s focus needs to be on protecting Canadian auto workers, not undermining them by importing even more state-subsidized cheap Chinese cars,” Ford said on social media on Monday.

Trump’s tariffs have battered Canada’s auto industry, potentially unraveling decades of cross-border integration. Canada recently threatened to sue Stellantis after the company moved its plans for Jeep Compass production from Ontario to Illinois and agreed to sell its idled Canadian assembly plant.

Carney said Saturday that he had spoken at length with Trump and senior U.S. officials and that the two countries were making progress toward a possible trade agreement, although differences remained.

items._ogDesc: Thousands of customers reported difficulty accessing online accounts at several major U.S. banks and the money transfer service Zelle on Monday after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects throughout the financial system.
items.body:
NEW YORK — Thousands of customers reported difficulty accessing online accounts at several major U.S. banks and the money transfer service Zelle on Monday after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects throughout the financial system.

However, Chase said Monday that the technical problems were not the result of a cyberattack, and that it was working to bring banking services back online.

“JPMorgan Chase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in an on-premise hardware system — it is not cyber-related,” said Joe Evangelisti, spokesman for the bank.

  • Latest updates on company news here

The disruption comes days after two major outages affected other parts of the U.S. economy: A major outage by Microsoft happened Thursday and lasted for hours, severely impacting services including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot. This was followed by an outage affecting the nation’s air traffic control system Friday that grounded all U.S. flights for several hours and continued to disrupt air travel across the country over the weekend.

In the same statement, Evangelisti said that this was a Chase-only issue.

“This is not a systemic issue — other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us,” he said.

Monday’s technical issues seem to be centered at Chase customers and customers at other banks trying to transact with Chase. Those banks, including Bank of America and Citigroup, were not having issues with their banking services.

A spokesman for U.S. Bank said its systems are not directly impacted but that “clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays.”

  • Latest updates on international news here

Zelle is the peer-to-peer payment system that major U.S. banks use to allow customers to send money to friends and family at near-instant speed. Zelle is owned by Arizona-based Early Warning Services, which in turn is owned by financial institutions including Bank of America, Capital One, JPMorgan Chase, PNC Bank, Truist, U.S. Bank and Wells Fargo.

A spokesman for Early Warning Services said the Zelle network was fully operational.

“An issue at the financial institutions may be delaying Zelle payments for some of their customers,” the spokesman said.

Some Chase customers received a message that said, “Some services aren’t available. We’re working on them. Please try back later.”

Cathy Bussewitz and Ken Sweet, The Associated Press

This story has been updated to correct Microsoft outage began Thursday, not Friday.

items.title: Stocks tumble on Wall Street as Nvidia leads another sell-off in technology companies
items.description: More drops for stocks in the artificial intelligence industry dragged the U.S. market lower on Monday, led by Nvidia.

items._ogDesc: More drops for stocks in the artificial intelligence industry dragged the U.S. market lower on Monday, led by Nvidia.
items.body:
NEW YORK — More drops for stocks in the artificial intelligence industry dragged the U.S. market lower on Monday, led by Nvidia.

The weakness for tech stocks helped knock the S&P 500 index 1.9 per cent lower and pushed the Nasdaq composite index to a 2.5 per cent loss. The Dow also fell sharply as losses broadened into other sectors. AI-focused companies were by far the biggest weights on the market and have been behind much of the recent turbulence on Wall Street.

Nvidia sank 4.1 per cent and was again the heaviest weight on Wall Street following its crisis of leadership. The company has lost US$735 billion in market value since the scandal erupted about CEO Jensen Huang’s infidelities and his ties to an alleged Chinese spy.

  • S&P 500 market updates here

Nvidia is one of the most influential companies in the world not only because its chips are powering much of the world’s move into AI technology but also because its cash has helped companies across the industry to grow.

Now, following Huang’s resignation as Nvidia’s CEO last week, both the chip company and the broad industry are facing a more uncertain future without the leather-jacketed man who became one of AI’s biggest celebrities.

It’s the latest challenge for the AI industry, which had already been shaken by criticism that stock prices in the industry shot too high and were in a bubble. The sweeping victories for Democrats in this month’s U.S. midterm elections also raised worries about possible restrictions on further construction of AI data centres.

“The market was already worried about this risk before what happened at Nvidia,” Zhiwei Zhang, president and chief economist at Pinpoint Asset Management, said in a commentary. “Now the risk has become even more serious.”

The sector is also now facing more scrutiny from the U.S. government. The Trump administration on Monday issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers.

Outside of Nvidia, other chip companies also fell. They had climbed in the earlier days of Nvidia’s fall on hopes that they could gain a competitive advantage. But Broadcom dropped 3.9 per cent and notched its second straight loss on concerns about the broader industry. Advanced Micro Devices fell 5.6 per cent.

CoreWeave, which buys Nvidia chips and then rents out access to them to customers over the cloud, sank 6.1 per cent. GE Vernova, which is helping to power AI data centres, fell 4.9 per cent.

  • Latest updates on artificial intelligence news here

The next big milestone for the AI industry may arrive Tuesday after trading in the U.S. stock market ends for the day. That’s when Nvidia will report its latest quarterly results, and interim CEO Colette Kress is set to speak to Wall Street. Investors have become accustomed to Nvidia not only reporting stronger results than analysts expected for each quarter but also giving a forecast for upcoming revenue that’s well above expectations.

Elsewhere on Wall Street, L3Harris Technologies fell 3.9 per cent after officials in President Donald Trump’s administration suggested the contractor for the Federal Aviation Administration may be at fault for a nationwide ground stop Friday. L3Harris said Saturday that it’s supporting the FAA in its investigation.

Summit Therapeutics sank 16.5 per cent after the biopharmaceutical company said the U.S. Food and Drug Administration indicated it cannot approve its application for a therapy to treat certain patients with lung cancer.

Tyson Foods rose 8.7 per cent after reporting a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. The company behind the Jimmy Dean and Hillshire Farm brands, though, also reported weaker revenue than expected after selling less beef than it did a year earlier.

Overall, the S&P 500 shed 145.08 points to close at 7,416.59, marking the third straight loss for the benchmark index. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 739.38 points, or 1.4 per cent, to 51,608.17. The Nasdaq composite fell 626.52 points to 24,509.76.

The recent swings for AI stocks have overshadowed what’s been another strong earnings reporting season for U.S. companies. The big businesses in the S&P 500 index are on track to deliver earnings per share for the summer nearly 32 per cent higher than a year earlier, according to FactSet.

It’s the third straight quarter of growth above 25 per cent for the index, which is important because corporate profits are one of the two big levers that set stock prices over the long term, along with interest rates.

  • Latest updates on investing here

In the bond market, Treasury yields eased back following last week’s jump due to a worse-than-expected report on U.S. inflation.

The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 5.13 per cent from 5.15 per cent late Friday, though it remains well above a low of 4.80 per cent reached earlier this month. Higher yields make borrowing money more expensive for everyone, and they’ve already hurt the housing industry through expensive mortgage rates.

Yields fell as oil prices sank, which took away some of the upward pressure on inflation. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil fell 3.5 per cent to US$92.44. It’s been yo-yoing amid uncertainty about what will happen in the war with Iran.

In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed in Europe.

Stan Choe, The Associated Press

(AP Photo/Heng Sinith)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Heng Sinith</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Prime Minister Mark Carney downplayed suggestions of a budding 'bromance' with Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, describing their relationship as friendly but professional.
items.body:
PHNOM PENH — Prime Minister Mark Carney downplayed suggestions of a budding “bromance” with Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, describing their relationship as friendly but professional.

The two leaders struck a cordial tone during their first meeting since the Parti Québécois formed government following last month’s provincial election, finding common ground on homelessness and economic co-operation. But differences remained over Quebec’s role in trade negotiations with the United States and its representation on the world stage.

“We will continue in a professional way — friendly but not necessarily a bromance. I have a wife,” Carney quipped in French at a news conference Monday in Phnom Penh, Cambodia.

His comments contrasted with the enthusiasm expressed by St-Pierre Plamondon, who described Sunday’s meeting on the sidelines of the Francophonie summit as “very pleasant and funny.”

“We certainly share a sense of humour,” the sovereigntist premier said in a statement published Sunday following the meeting.

St-Pierre Plamondon said the two leaders had found common ground on several issues, exchanged personal phone numbers and agreed to meet again in the coming weeks.

Carney said the two leaders had plenty of work ahead of them, pointing to homelessness and major infrastructure projects, including Contrecœur and Churchill Falls.

Carney’s meeting with St-Pierre Plamondon in Cambodia came after a few weeks of friction between the two men since the Quebec premier’s victory in the Oct. 5 provincial election.

They initially could not agree over the location of their meeting. While Carney offered to meet in Montreal or the Ottawa-Gatineau region, St-Pierre Plamondon had argued that the meeting should take place in Quebec City.

  • ‘Asking Quebec to fall in line’: Quebec premier skips Canada-EU Summit

The Quebec premier also declined to attend Canada’s October summit with the European Union in Montreal saying the federal government had denied him an opportunity to deliver an official speech.

But both leaders appeared to be more collaborative after meeting in Cambodia.

On homelessness, St-Pierre Plamondon said in his statement that Carney had agreed to let Quebec choose projects and co-ordinate funding through a summit the province is organizing.

The Quebec premier also welcomed Carney’s support for an economic gathering Quebec plans to host in 2027, bringing together economy and foreign trade ministers from French-speaking countries, along with businesses.

St-Pierre Plamondon described the initiative as an opportunity to diversify Quebec’s economy and strengthen economic ties within the Francophonie.

But the two leaders appeared to have different views on Quebec’s role in negotiations with the United States.

St-Pierre Plamondon wants Quebec to have a greater say in trade discussions, while Carney maintained that international agreements are negotiated by the federal government.

“I understand stakeholders making their views known to those in the United States, and it’s important to get those views across,” Carney said. “International agreements are negotiated between federal governments.”

Carney said Quebec could communicate with American counterparts and reiterated his commitment to sharing information with the province, as Ottawa does with other provincial governments.

The prime minister also rejected the idea of Quebec obtaining additional independent seats in international organizations.

He pointed to Quebec’s existing status within the International Organisation of La Francophonie, where the province participates as a full member.

Quebec has also had official representation within Canada’s Permanent Delegation to UNESCO since 2006, allowing it to participate in discussions on culture and education, areas under provincial jurisdiction.

“Canada has an enormous impact on the world stage,” Carney said in French, pointing to its participation in the Francophonie, Commonwealth, G20 and G7, as well as its relations with the European Union.

“We advance objectives for all Canadians,” he added.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 16, 2026.

Caroline Plante, The Canadian Press

items._ogDesc: Canadian inflation held at 3.1% in October, while property taxes rose 3.8%, outpacing overall price growth as Ontario tax arrears climbed.
items.body:
Canada’s headline inflation remains elevated, but at least it didn’t get worse. Statistics Canada (StatCan) data shows annual headline CPI growth held at 3.1% in October. The lack of acceleration would be good news if not for broadening inflation. Core measures didn’t clarify much this month, but one thing was clear—property taxes are still ripping while arrears climb.

Canadian Inflation Holds At 3.1%, Tamed By Cooling Gas Prices

Annual CPI growth rate.

Annual growth of CPI held at 3.1% in October, remaining elevated but unchanged from September. Helping to tame growth was a deceleration in gasoline prices, which fell 2.5% in the month but were up 30.9% from last year. The agency also notes that annual declines for cellphone plans (-6.2%) helped, though prices may not be lower. Cell phone plans have been a persistent downward pressure due to methodology, not because people are paying less.

Hard Core? Canada’s “Stable” Core CPI Measures Moved Lower, Higher, and Stalled

Canada’s Core CPI measures are designed to provide some clarity, and minimize headline volatility. Unfortunately, Canada’s three big core measures all told a different story last month.

CPI median’s annual growth was unchanged at 2.0%. The core measure tracks the midpoint of price changes, weighted by spending.

CPI-trim slowed from 1.9% to 1.8% in October. This measure excludes the largest upward and downward movements, ideally eliminating the volatility. In practice, prices take the elevator up and the stairs down. As a result, much larger price surges can be neutralized by much smaller declines.

CPI-common accelerated to 2.5% y/y in October, up from 2.4% in September. This measure tracks price movements across categories, filtering out fluctuations for individual items.

No measure is perfect, and the mixed direction reveals how flawed the shift to annual re-indexing has been. The agency’s Census intervals are spaced out to minimize the volatility of resource allocation. However, StatCan argues the pricing of those resources needs to be re-indexed annually.

Canadian Property Tax Growth Slows, But Still Faster Than Inflation

Annual growth of property taxes and special charges.

Every October StatCan’s CPI reports property taxes and other special charges. The segment saw prices rise 3.8% from last year, down from 5.6% reported in 2025. Slower than recent years, but it’s coming down from the sharpest surge since the early ’90s. At the same time, it’s nearly double the BoC’s target rate of inflation, and well above its upper bound of tolerance.

Slower-but-still-elevated property tax and special charges are also unlikely to feel like relief. The 3.3% annual growth in Ontario follows last year’s 5.5% jump. It’s been accompanied by a sharp rise in property tax arrears. Recent filings in the region reveal a property tax arrears rate of up to 11.9% in its largest municipalities.

items.title: When will Canada’s housing market finally bounce back?
items.description: It’s been more of the same for the Canadian housing outlook in 2026. Will 2027 bring a change?
items.content: <p>It’s been more of the same for the Canadian housing outlook in 2026. Will 2027 bring a change?</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639298402582987630.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: It’s been more of the same for the Canadian housing outlook in 2026. Will 2027 bring a change?
items.body:
Fall activity in Canada’s housing market has remained muted as affordability challenges and economic unease continue to roil the sector, with little chance of a pickup in momentum before the end of 2026.

A recent analysis by RBC Economics described a housing market recovery as “shaky at best” over the past several weeks, marked by even or declining home values and virtually no uptick in sales.

The main reasons for that will come as no surprise to mortgage market watchers: the trade war with the US is still rumbling on, while interest rates have been on the up and immigration numbers have dwindled.

There’s been some room for optimism on the trade front in November, with prime minister Mark Carney and US president Donald Trump suggesting both sides were working towards an agreement to end the tariff dispute.

But the combination of the Bank of Canada’s recent interest rate increase and continued economic turbulence south of the border mean a recovery in the housing and mortgage markets could still be some distance away, according to Ownright co-founder and chief operating officer Joel Fox.

“Until we see a rate drop, I’d be quite surprised if we started to see year-over-year growth in the market,” Fox told Canadian Mortgage Professional. “The rate hike just really cemented that.”

US election provides ‘glimmer of hope’ but obstacles remain

The BoC’s latest decision saw it move off the sidelines for the first time in over three years, raising rates by 25 basis points as inflation fears harden amid the ongoing US-Iran conflict.

Still, Fox acknowledged reasons for guarded optimism following the US midterm election results, which saw the Democratic Party reclaim both the House and Senate and stirred hopes of renewed efforts to bring the trade conflict to a close.

But the unpredictable nature of US politics and the current administration also means it’s too soon to say whether a definitive end to tariff tensions is near, he added.

“There’s a glimmer of hope that we might be able to get to something with the US, which I think both they and us really, really want to see happen,” he said. “That said, we’ve of course seen that before – and then it all went belly up fast.”

Expectations continue to ramp down for Canada’s housing market

The sluggish pace of homebuying activity and continuing economic anxiety have seen forecasters including the Canadian Real Estate Association (CREA) adjust their expectations for the housing market this year and next.

In October, the association revealed it had lowered its home sales forecast for the third quarter in a row, slashing 18,806 sales from its July expectations and now projecting overall sales for the year to slip 5.2% from 2025.

CREA said it now expected national average 2026 home prices to increase at a slower pace than previously anticipated, with forecasts of a slightly improved outlook for next year “predicated on slow but positive economic growth, the resumption of higher population growth, and more certainty for borrowers around the path for interest rates.”

Those factors, the association said, should move pent-up demand off the sidelines even as borrowing costs continue to jump.

Unsurprisingly, real estate and mortgage industry sentiment has also adjusted, with the belief that a market bounce-back was just around the corner now giving way to a less bullish approach. Fox said he’s noticed that among referral partners including real estate agents and mortgage brokers.

“Within the past two or three months, that optimism just doesn’t seem to be there – which is shocking, because [it’s] always felt like it’s been there,” he said.

While the COVID-19 pandemic marked a lucrative time to be employed in Canadian real estate, bringing with it a flood of new entrants into the realtor profession, many of those who joined during that era are now having second thoughts about their future.

“The COVID boom brought a lot of realtors into the market, and everything that’s happened since then is continuing to drive folks out,” he said. “You’ve got professionals in the space that are finding a way to work in this market – but there’s just not enough business to go around for everyone else.”

items.content: <p>Mortgage agent on how she’s helping new buyers break into the market</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0343_639304466007678370.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Mortgage agent on how she’s helping new buyers break into the market
items.body:
First-time buyers who spent years on the sidelines are finally getting into the market as affordability improves and purchase competition eases. We caught up with Mortgage Powered Financial Group mortgage agent Sarita Free at MortgageFest to hear how she’s helping borrowers navigate the current environment.

[00:00] They're finally able to break into the market and stay in their hometown where they've grown up and not have to go elsewhere. It's huge. It helps them qualify for a little bit more. Again, work your book, know your clients. Nothing's just going to be handed to you. So, 2027 is going to be what you make it as a broker.

[00:26] Fergal McAlinden: All right. Well, next up we have our first mortgage agent of the day. We've talked only with lenders so far. So, today we're really happy to have Sarita Free with Mortgage Powered Financial Group.

[00:36] Sarita Free: Yep. It's a mouthful, but you got it.

[00:39] Fergal McAlinden: Good stuff. Is it useful for you as an agent to speak with lenders, get some facetime? I mean, there's a lot of them here today. What type of conversation have you been having?

[00:46] Sarita Free: Well, to be quite honest, I haven't been able to get right in. I'd like to go see some of the tech companies to be fully transparent. Anything that makes my job easier, especially with AI coming out and just stuff to streamline my process.

[01:00] Fergal McAlinden: How about the market so far this year, 2026? We all know it's been an interesting outlook for agents and lenders and everyone. How are you navigating it and what are some of the main things you've been seeing?

[01:11] Sarita Free: Obviously I think my market is special. I'm in Norfolk County, Ontario, and our prices have been pretty stable. A lot of my clients are first-time home buyers and they've finally been able to break in. I am seeing a lot more alternative files on my desk, which is fitting because I'm moderating the alternative panel later. [laughter]

[01:28] Fergal McAlinden: For first-time home buyers, I know for a lot of them this has been kind of the light at the end of the tunnel after what we've been seeing over the past few years. Suddenly, they're in a position to buy. Has that been a big change for you this year?

[01:38] Sarita Free: My book typically has been a lot of first-time home buyers, but yes, this year I'm finding that they're finally able to get into the market. Norfolk County has some great home ownership programs as well. And again, with the 30-year amortization that we can now go to, I find a lot of my buyers that have been on the sidelines, they're finally able to break into the market and stay in their hometown where they've grown up and not have to go elsewhere.

[02:04] Which is huge. Norfolk County, again, it's a special place.

[02:06] Fergal McAlinden: For sure. And that's something that we haven't always seen. People looking to buy have had to go further afield. They haven't been able to stay where they are.

[02:13] Sarita Free: Like a couple of years ago when there were multiple offers and bidding wars. It was so disheartening to have these conversations with people whose family has been in our county for decades and them not being able to break in. So, this year has been really heartwarming and last year, too.

[02:32] Fergal McAlinden: That 30-year amortization is something that I wanted to ask you about. It's really interesting to hear that so many are using that. I know there was a little bit of skepticism about it when it was first unveiled, but every agent and broker that I've spoken to says that's been a really big game changer for buyers.

[02:46] Sarita Free: Yeah, it's huge. It helps them qualify for a little bit more. It makes the payments a little bit more manageable. So it's come in really handy. I'd like to see it in the insurable space. Maybe.

[02:59] Fergal McAlinden: We'll see.

[03:00] Sarita Free: We can hope.

[03:01] Fergal McAlinden: Anything else for first-time buyers? Any other kinds of trends across your desk when you're dealing with them? Are price points okay for them?

[03:09] Sarita Free: Yeah, I think price points are good right now. In more broader markets things have kind of leveled out. Norfolk County as well. I'm really passionate about Norfolk County. It's a smaller market and the majority of my book is there. So, it's a lot different than Toronto and the GTA, but yeah, prices are great and they've absolutely been able to get into the market. It's more affordable now.

[03:31] I don't see bidding wars. And when you do that little trick where realtors price a house really low hoping for that, it does not fly where I'm from.

[03:42] Fergal McAlinden: So, they've got a little bit of time to weigh up their offer and see the property and all that kind of thing.

[03:46] Sarita Free: Exactly. Which is great. Conditions of finance are back in. In-home inspections, everything. You name it. Water testing.

[03:53] Fergal McAlinden: Yeah. We have price reductions, upgrade the electrical, I want a new septic tank.

[03:57] Sarita Free: It's such a good outlook for first-time buyers, which is great.

[04:01] Fergal McAlinden: But it's been a challenging market in some other ways for other buyers and other homeowners as well. We know that renewals are still a big challenge for a lot of people.

[04:10] Sarita Free: Oh, yeah. I see on renewals right now a lot of clients extending their amortization out if it's possible. Going from a jump of an interest rate, goodness, like I had one across my desk the other day, 1.1 to now much higher. Definitely amortizations are being extended in some cases.

[04:28] Fergal McAlinden: That's great. Is there anything this year that you've been keeping top of mind as a broker that maybe wasn't a focus in previous years, or any advice that you would have for agents and brokers navigating the current market?

[04:37] Sarita Free: Right now, work your book. I know you've probably heard that from other agents, but work your book. Stay in contact with your clients. Look for opportunities where their rate might be high. Look for opportunities where they could switch to a new lender for a lower rate. Maybe give them some kind of relief, or refinances, all that kind of stuff. Again, work your book, know your clients.

[05:00] Fergal McAlinden: I'm really interested in hearing from you as an agent. AI, how have you been using that? Has it been a game changer for you? Are you skeptical about it? What way are you approaching it?

[05:09] Sarita Free: No, I'm not skeptical. I think I'm still going to hand in all my files, underwrite all my files, but I'm looking for ways to maybe streamline and speed up repetitive administrative kind of tasks.

[05:22] And actually, I'm interested to see who we have here today that could talk to us about AI. I think there's a panel on AI today, right?

[05:30] Fergal McAlinden: Yes. How about whenever you're looking into your crystal ball, as we say, what do you think is in store for 2027? Are you expecting a busier market or more of the same? What are your thoughts?

[05:41] Sarita Free: I do think it's going to stay steady and get busier, but we're in sales. You get out of it what you put in, right? So, if you want to have a busy 2027, you have to work for it now. Nothing's just going to be handed to you.

[05:55] It doesn't matter. We're in the business of not only purchases and sales, but refinances and switches. There's lots of business out there to be had for every single one of us brokers, every one of us in the room today. So, 2027 is going to be what you make it as a broker.

[06:12] Fergal McAlinden: That's great. Well, thank you very much for joining us today. Really appreciate it, Sarita, and all the best with your panel later on.

[06:18] Sarita Free: Thank you so much.

items.description: Canada’s central bank kicks off its governor search as Macklem rules out a second term
items.content: <p>Canada’s central bank kicks off its governor search as Macklem rules out a second term</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639304443759641224.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Canada’s central bank kicks off its governor search as Macklem rules out a second term
items.body:
Tiff Macklem, the 10th Governor of the Bank of Canada, confirmed Monday he will not seek a second term when his seven-year mandate expires on June 2, 2027.

The Bank’s board has formed a search committee assisted by Zurich-based executive recruiting firm Egon Zehnder, with results expected by spring 2027.

The new governor will be formally appointed by Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne and Prime Minister Mark Carney — himself a former Bank of Canada governor — to take office on June 3, 2027.

“It has been the highlight of my career to serve as the 10th Governor of the Bank of Canada,” Macklem said.

“My time as Governor has seen Canada navigate a more fragmented, shock-prone world. The Bank has faced these challenges by acting decisively, by using sound judgment in the face of uncertainty, and by serving Canadians with humility and a steadfast commitment to its mandate.”

Macklem, 65, took the role on June 3, 2020, with the overnight rate already cut to 0.25% and an emergency bond-purchasing program underway.

His departure was widely expected; no governor had served a second term since 1980.

A legacy shaped by historic rate swings

The defining feature of Macklem’s tenure was Canada’s inflation fight. Consumer prices peaked at 8.1% in mid-2022, prompting one of the Bank’s most aggressive tightening cycles on record — 10 consecutive hikes over 16 months lifted the policy rate from 0.25% to 5%.

After cutting rates, the Bank raised again to 2.5% on October 28, its first hike since 2023.

Jessica Rickerby, president of the Canadian Mortgage Brokers Association of Ontario (CMBA Ontario) in Toronto, said after that move: “While inflation is a key concern of Ontarians, so is housing affordability. The difference is that affordability is a pressing issue right now, whereas inflation is — at present — a hypothetical.”

Who could lead the Bank next — and what it means for brokers

The Bank’s 14-page executive brief for the role sets a high bar for candidates.

Applicants must hold Canadian citizenship and a graduate-level degree in economics, speak both official languages at a high level, and bring experience at the most senior levels of central banking, public policy, financial regulation, or international institutions.

The board has partnered with Quebec economists who joined the Bank of Canada’s inner circle in 2026 and other senior policymakers in shaping the institution Macklem leaves behind.

For brokers navigating Canada’s mounting 2026 mortgage renewal pressures, the transition carries direct weight.

Bruno Valko, vice-president of national sales at RMG Mortgage Corporation in Toronto, recently questioned the Bank’s inflation outlook: “Come 2027, when comparing oil prices to 2026, assuming oil continues to hover around $100 per barrel, I dispute the rationale around how inflation can average 3% when it’s currently 3.1%.”

items.title: Bank Of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem Stepping Down
items.description:
Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem is stepping down next June.

The Bank’s Board of Directors announced Monday that Macklem has told them he won’t seek a second term when his seven-year term ends on June 2, 2027.

The Board has started a search for the next Governor.

“It has been the highlight of my career to serve as the 10th Governor of the Bank of Canada,” Macklem said. “My time as Governor has seen Canada navigate a more fragmented, shock-prone world. The Bank has faced these challenges by acting decisively, by using sound judgment in the face of uncertainty, and by serving Canadians with humility and a steadfast commitment to its mandate.”

Macklem thanked the Board, the Minister of Finance, and the Prime Minister for entrusting him with the stewardship of Canada’s central bank.

“It is a privilege to serve as Governor, and I remain fully committed to fulfilling my responsibilities and delivering for Canadians through the remainder of my term,” he said.

The independent directors on the Board have formed a Search Committee to run the recruitment process. Executive recruiting firm Egon Zehnder is helping them, and the Bank is inviting interested candidates to read the Executive Brief for the role and contact Egon Zehnder confidentially.

The Bank expects to finish the search by spring 2027.

Subject to approval from the Minister of Finance and federal Cabinet, the Board’s independent directors will appoint the next Governor to a seven-year term starting June 3, 2027.

items.content: <p>New immigration levels won’t overwhelm housing, but Canada’s supply gap stands at 571,000 units</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639304410184682267.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: New immigration levels won’t overwhelm housing, but Canada’s supply gap stands at 571,000 units
items.body:
Canada’s residential construction sector is running at a pace sufficient to absorb projected 2027 population growth under the federal government’s new immigration plan, but a supply deficit built during the 2022–2024 surge will take years to clear.

That is the central finding of a new analysis by Rentals.ca, which used Statistics Canada population estimates alongside Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) housing starts and completions data to establish an absorption benchmark.

“At the current pace of about 240,000 starts a year, absorption capacity is approximately 500,000 people,” the report said, based on the ratio that kept supply aligned with population from 1990 to 2015.

Budget 2026 introduced a new immigration levels plan for 2027 to 2029, setting permanent resident admissions at 380,000 annually and adding up to 282,000 one-time and time-limited transitions alongside 370,000 new temporary resident arrivals.

Because most transitions target individuals already residing in Canada, net population growth will be narrower than the headline figures imply.

The report said projected 2027 population growth of 177,000 to 440,000 falls below the 500,000-person absorption capacity of current construction in every scenario modelled.

Kevin Fettig of CMI Financial Group says Budget 2026's housing reforms could improve access to financing for smaller developers, but municipal zoning and approval delays must also be addressed to boost supply. https://t.co/KjzLNLNcY7 — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) November 11, 2026

The gap left by the 2022–2024 surge

The near-term outlook does not resolve Canada’s deeper structural challenge. The cumulative supply gap — measuring units required above those started to maintain historical construction-to-population ratios — peaked at approximately 780,000 units in mid-2024.

“With population growth slowing and starts holding near 240,000 a year, the gap narrowed to about 571,000 units as of mid-2026,” the report said.

As CMHC’s Fall 2026 Housing Supply Report showed, Canada still requires an estimated 187,000 to 238,000 additional units per year beyond current construction to restore affordability.

Closing the existing deficit under the lowest-growth scenario would take nearly four years of construction above population requirements; under the high-growth scenario, more than a decade.

Construction slowdown may delay rent relief

The report said average national asking rents have declined on an annual basis for 25 consecutive months and are down 5.4% over two years, while the national purpose-built rental vacancy rate climbed to 3.1% in 2025, above its 10-year average.

That cushion is already narrowing: “Asking rents in Toronto and Vancouver are rising for the first time in nearly three years, and the collapse in condo presales will reduce completions in 2028 and 2029,” the report said.

Mathieu Laberge, Chief Economist and Senior Vice President at CMHC in Ottawa, addressed the construction risk directly at the recent Mortgage Professionals Canada National conference in Calgary.

“If we react to a softer market by stopping too much construction, we may be protecting ourselves from today’s risks — but we’re also creating tomorrow’s shortages,” he warned.

“We are at a very high risk that by not providing the appropriate and sufficient supply today, we will lose the improvement in affordability we’ve seen two or three, or five years down the road.”

Laberge also pointed to a structural mismatch in what is being built: “Canada doesn’t simply have too much or too little housing. The reality is that we have a mismatch between the homes people need and the homes the system is producing. What’s small is unaffordable and what’s large is unavailable.”

For brokers advising clients on purchase timing and rental strategy, the report cautioned that newly permanent residents are likely to accelerate household formation, pushing vacancy rates lower before the pipeline fully catches up.

“Pressure on rents and vacancy rates that built up during the surge is therefore likely to ease more gradually than previously projected,” it said.

The bottom line for brokers

The report is broadly constructive in one sense — 2027 isn’t going to see a repeat of the 2022–2024 demand shock. But it is not a signal that the structural supply problem is solved.

The practical read for brokers is that the market remains undersupplied relative to long-run need, rent relief is fragile, and a new cohort of newly permanent residents is about to start forming households and entering the mortgage market.

Getting in front of that client segment now, while also managing the renewal and purchase conversations shaped by a persistent gap, is where the opportunity sits.

items.title: Commission scheme costs former BC realtor his licence and $627,000
items.description: Regulator details kickbacks, a fake inspection and deleted emails behind the penalty
items.content: <p>Regulator details kickbacks, a fake inspection and deleted emails behind the penalty</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0311_638563834459414345.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Regulator details kickbacks, a fake inspection and deleted emails behind the penalty
items.body:
A former Squamish, BC, real estate agent who funnelled buyers to two colleagues in exchange for kickbacks must pay $627,000.

The BC Financial Services Authority (BCFSA) also cancelled his licence in a sanctions decision dated Oct. 28 and made public Nov. 13.

The order against Andre Zubko and his personal real estate corporation stems from a commission scheme he ran across eight home sales in 2016 and 2017. It combines $320,000 in discipline penalties with $307,000 in enforcement expenses.

Zubko’s licence renewal was denied in 2017, and he has not been licensed since.

How did the commission scheme work?

Zubko was licensed from 2006 to 2017 and worked at One Percent Realty, a flat-fee brokerage.

According to the decision, he sent unrepresented buyers to a high school acquaintance and to a cousin of a family member. Those agents wrote offers demanding a higher buyer’s commission, then passed most of it back to him.

Sellers paid more than $50,000 in extra commissions, and Zubko collected $47,641.23 in kickbacks.

Two deals went further. In one, Zubko persuaded a seller to cut the price of a lot sold to his family member from $350,000 to $175,000. The contract was assigned days later for $335,000, a $160,000 gain.

In another, he invented a home inspection to push a price down from $807,000 to $797,000, even though he knew the contract had already been assigned for $845,000.

“It is difficult to imagine a more clear-cut case of deception of one’s client than completely making up a negative home inspection in order to convince that client to sell their property at a lower price,” Senior Hearing Officer Andrew Pendray wrote.

During the investigation, Zubko deleted emails, met with others involved to align their accounts, and gave investigators false statements.

Canadian Mortgage Professional reported the regulator’s original misconduct findings in 2024. 

FSRA's has permanently removed a former mortgage agent's licence and imposed administrative penalties after findings related to unlicensed mortgage activity, improper compensation arrangements, and facilitating dishonesty. https://t.co/Wjos9A5fUi — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) November 3, 2026

What the penalty signals for BC brokers

Four transactions fell under the rules in force before Sept. 30, 2016, which capped penalties at $10,000.

For the remaining four, Pendray assessed $550,000, then cut it by 50% to $275,000. He cited proportionality and Zubko’s years without a licence.

He added $35,000 to strip out any remaining profit and set enforcement costs at 65% of the regulator’s expenses.

Zubko had proposed about $85,000 in penalties and $40,000 in costs.

Limiting fines to client losses, Pendray wrote, would turn them into “just the cost of doing business in an inappropriate way, and only if one was caught.”

The ruling lands weeks after BC’s Mortgage Services Act took effect on Oct. 13, completing the province’s overhaul of mortgage broker regulation.

The regulator has also acted against individual brokers, including one barred for falsifying clients’ income records. 

Zubko has 30 days from the decision to appeal to the Financial Services Tribunal and 60 days to pay.

items.title: October inflation steady, complicating BoC’s December call
items.description: Canada’s October CPI held flat, raising doubts over another Bank of Canada rate hike
items.content: <p>Canada’s October CPI held flat, raising doubts over another Bank of Canada rate hike</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639304381242559284.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Canada’s October CPI held flat, raising doubts over another Bank of Canada rate hike
items.body:
Canada’s annual inflation rate held at 3.1% in October, matching September’s reading and coming in just below the 3.2% most economists had expected. The data has now tilted the debate toward a potential pause at the Bank of Canada’s (BoC) December 9 rate decision.

Statistics Canada reported Monday that the consumer price index (CPI) rose 0.2% on a seasonally adjusted basis month over month in October.

Upward pressure from gasoline, groceries, clothing, and natural gas was partially offset by cheaper cell phone plans and slower rent growth.

Excluding energy, the CPI rose 2.0% year over year, edging down from 2.1% in September.

Gasoline remained the dominant inflationary driver, rising 30.9% year over year from 27.8% in September, reflecting a base-year effect tied to lower crude oil prices in October 2025.

Despite that headline figure, pump prices fell 2.5% month over month. Grocery price growth ticked up to 2.0% year over year from 1.7%, breaking a four-month easing streak, with fresh vegetable prices rising 1.4% after declining 2.9% in September.

Clothing costs climbed 1.8% year over year, the largest monthly increase since September 2019, with Statistics Canada attributing the move to higher shipping costs.

Excluding food and energy, the CPI eased to 1.8% year over year.

Canada’s labour market shed 4,700 jobs in October, pushing the national unemployment rate to 6.7% from 6.5%, a third consecutive month of deterioration that is now complicating the Bank of Canada’s (BoC) path to a December rate hike. https://t.co/M8Ce4IYrjH — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) November 10, 2026

Economists split on December

The BoC’s preferred core measures — CPI-trim at 1.8% and CPI-median at 2.0% year over year — held at or below the 2% target. The case for holding at December 9 has strengthened, though the question is not fully settled.

Andrew Grantham, senior economist at CIBC Economics in Toronto, was direct: “Today’s tame inflation report, combined with the recent move lower in gasoline prices and signs of weakness in the labour market, suggest that there’s no need for the Bank of Canada to rush another interest rate hike and supports our call for a hold in December.”

RBC Economics’ Abbey Xu, based in Toronto, retained a more cautious outlook. Her base case remains a 25-basis-point hike to 2.75% at the December meeting, “although further downside surprises in growth, employment or inflation could still give policymakers reason to pause.”

Leslie Preston, senior economist at TD Economics in Toronto, characterised the BoC’s October 28 move to 2.5% as pre-emptive: “The Bank of Canada raised interest rates in October to get ahead of an expected uptick in inflation in Canada, but the signs of hotter price gains were fairly lukewarm in October.”

What it means for brokers

Bond yields and the Canadian dollar both fell Monday following the release, signalling that markets are trimming expectations of a December hike.

For mortgage professionals across Canada, the December 9 announcement will carry unusual weight for client conversations and product strategy.

Three consecutive monthly job losses, softer-than-expected third-quarter GDP growth, and declining gasoline prices, as flagged by RBC’s Xu, now all argue for patience from the BoC.

Whether core inflation broadens enough over the next three weeks to justify another rate increase will determine whether Canada’s mortgage market greets 2027 at 2.5% or 2.75%.

items.body:
Time for your cheat sheet on this week’s top stories.

Canadian Real Estate

Canadian Immigration Changes To Double Population Growth Rate: BMO

Canada’s looking to boost its immigration, but it hasn’t framed it that way. Officially, the target is to add 380,000 new permanent residents per year for 2027-29. However, BMO economists estimate that special measures push the total to 660,000 for 2027. The massive change has the bank nearly doubling its population growth forecast. Though it’s worth distinguishing between a target and reality. Canada’s foreign student tapering only began after applications dropped sharply, suggesting exhausted demand.

Canadian Housing Affordability’s Record Recovery May End Soon: NBF

Housing affordability across Canada has made a record 11 straight quarters of improvement. That sounds impressive, but the details are less flattering. Mortgage payments on a typical home would consume 50.9% of a median household’s income at this level. Even with the record length of improvements, this is still one of the worst markets for buyers in history. National Bank economists warn this may also be as good as it gets in the near-term, as mortgage rates are set to climb.

Canada To Add 200,000 Permanent Resident Spots, Housing Boost Limited

Canada’s immigration plan will boost permanent residents 50% higher than the headline data suggests. It’s seen as a boost to the economy, especially housing demand, but that may not be the case. The added capacity targets those already in the country and looking to stay. While this can mean less churn and ultimately more people, demand doesn’t get a direct boost. Their consumption is already reflected in the current data.

Ontario Real Estate

Ontario Property Tax Arrears Hit 24-Year High, Brampton Leads At 11.9%

Ontario property tax arrears are at a 24-year high, driven by Toronto’s suburbs. Filings show the property tax arrears rate hit 7.2% of the $34.1 billion in levies for 2025, up 2.46 points since 2019. The rate is now at its highest level since 2001, but there’s an important distinction here. Today, the rate is climbing, but back then it was falling after the early ‘90s real estate bubble popped. Coincidentally, property taxes just made their biggest increase since the early ’90s.

Toronto Real Estate

Over 1 In 8 Greater Toronto Rental Units Sit Vacant As Completions Hit A Record

Greater Toronto’s rental construction boom means a lot of supply is sitting empty. The often-reported vacancy rate for stabilized purpose-built rentals fell from 5.4% to 3.0% in Q3. The catch is stabilized, which excludes buildings that have never hit 95% occupancy. In a normal market, it may not be a big difference; including all purpose-built units means a 13.3% vacancy rate. Even with 1 in 8 units vacant, there are 34,545 more currently under construction, nearly half of the units being built across Canada. So far, there’s been minimal progress on prices, but that can change fast with a record supply glut on the way.
